## Penn World Table and Maddison: reuse the tables already in memory

```python
# Penn World Table and Maddison: already in memory from B.9
us_pwt = pwt[pwt["countrycode"] == "USA"].copy()
us_pwt["gdp_pc"] = us_pwt["rgdpna"] / us_pwt["pop"]
pwt_pc = us_pwt.set_index("year")["gdp_pc"].rename("Penn World Table")
pwt_pc.index = pwt_pc.index.astype(int)

mad_pc = maddison[maddison["countrycode"] == "USA"].set_index("year")["gdppc"].rename("Maddison")

# One table: pd.concat puts the five columns side by side, matching the years
sources = pd.concat([fred_pc, wb_pc, imf_pc, pwt_pc, mad_pc], axis=1).sort_index()
sources.loc[2000:]
```

[`pd.concat(..., axis=1)` matches the five Series on their year index, leaving `NaN` where a source has no value.]{.comment .fragment}

::: {.notes}
.copy() avoids pandas' warning about modifying a slice. The PWT years arrive as floating-point numbers from the Stata file, so .astype(int) makes them integers like the other indexes. Without that, 2000.0 and 2000 would still match, but the table would print oddly.

No download here: the Penn World Table and Maddison tables are already in memory, the polite way to use servers (good habit).
:::

## Five columns, five units: the levels cannot be compared directly

::: {.output}
```text
          FRED    World Bank       IMF WEO  Penn World Table      Maddison
2000  49914.50  48616.254628  49933.506536      55171.319764  45886.470498
...
2010  54188.25  52812.682987  54206.538072      59465.698228  49266.915862
...
2020  61127.00  59533.609024  61225.660175      65783.138914  54379.206512
2021  64828.50  63096.785615  64839.516732      69617.537868  57522.704626
2022  66037.25  64322.233282  66057.138042      71079.677954  58487.465861
2023  67412.25  65667.281580  67438.383199      72718.486651           NaN
2024  68788.50  66856.513170  68810.761710               NaN           NaN
2025  70020.25  67945.614650  70032.247214               NaN           NaN
...
2031       NaN           NaN  77616.076824               NaN           NaN
```
:::

[In 2000 the levels range from about \$45,900 (Maddison) to \$55,200 (Penn World Table).]{.comment .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Trimmed to a few years. The last year with all five sources is 2022: Maddison ends in 2022, the Penn World Table in 2023, the official sources in 2025, the IMF forecasts in 2031.

The level differences come from units (base years, PPP dollars) and from population estimates. They say nothing about growth. To compare growth, we index.
:::

## Index each source to 2000 = 100, then compute average growth

::: {.eqpanel}
$$\text{index}_t = 100 \times \frac{y_t}{y_{2000}} \qquad g = \left(\frac{y_{\text{end}}}{y_{2000}}\right)^{1/(\text{end} - 2000)} - 1$$
:::

```python
END = int(sources.dropna().index.max())       # the last year with all five sources
index = 100 * sources.loc[2000:END] / sources.loc[2000]
growth = 100 * ((sources.loc[END] / sources.loc[2000]) ** (1 / (END - 2000)) - 1)
print(f"Average annual growth of U.S. real GDP per person, 2000-{END}, percent:")
print(growth.round(2).to_string())
```

::: {.incremental}
- An index removes the units: every source starts at 100.
- $g$ is the constant yearly growth rate that takes $y_{2000}$ to $y_{\text{end}}$.
:::

::: {.notes}
sources.dropna() keeps the years with all five values; .index.max() is the last of them, 2022. Dividing a table by one row (sources.loc[2000]) divides each column by its own 2000 value.

The growth formula is the average annual growth rate of Chapter 3: the constant rate g such that y_2000 × (1 + g)^(end − 2000) = y_end.
:::

## Will the five sources agree on the growth rate?

[Same country, same years, same concept. Will the five average growth rates for 2000–2022 be equal, almost equal, or clearly different? Which sources will agree?]{.predict-output}

::: {.notes}
Give students a minute to commit to an answer, ideally in writing. Then reveal the output. Hint for discussion: think of which sources copy the latest official U.S. numbers and which rebuild them every few years.
:::

## Three sources say 1.28% a year; the research datasets say less

::: {.output}
```text
Average annual growth of U.S. real GDP per person, 2000-2022, percent:
FRED                1.28
World Bank          1.28
IMF WEO             1.28
Penn World Table    1.16
Maddison            1.11
```
:::

::: {.incremental}
- FRED, the World Bank and the IMF agree **exactly**: [1.28%]{.key}. All three copy the latest official U.S. numbers.
- The Penn World Table ([1.16%]{.key}) and the Maddison Project ([1.11%]{.key}) show slower growth.
- The gap: 0.17 percentage points a year, every year, for 22 years.
:::

::: {.notes}
The numbers of the hook, now explained by the code that made them.

The gap is in percentage points, not percent: 1.28 − 1.11 = 0.17 points. Over 22 years a small yearly gap adds up to a visible difference in the index, as the chart shows.
:::

[Where in the 22 years do the five lines part ways: at once, slowly, or after one event?]{.question}

::: {.notes}
Ask students to look for the moment the Penn World Table and Maddison lines fall below the other three.
:::

## Why sources differ: vintages, population and prices

::: {.incremental}
- **Vintages.** Each source copied the official U.S. numbers at a different time, and the BEA revises GDP every year. FRED updates within days; the Penn World Table and Maddison every few years.
- **Population.** GDP per person divides by population, and the sources use different estimates (Census Bureau, United Nations, their own).
- **Prices and methods.** Different base years and, for the Penn World Table and Maddison, their own international prices.
:::

[Always say where a number comes from, and compare sources when a result matters.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The three reasons of B.10, which are the three ideas of Act I in action: vintages (Idea 3), units and prices (Idea 2), and the exact series behind a name (Idea 1).

The Zimbabwe population comparison of Act V is the same mechanism on a smaller scale: 15.2 million in Maddison against 16.1 million in the Penn World Table.
:::

## Different sources do not mean one of them is wrong

[The sources disagree, so one of them must have made a mistake.]{.myth}

[All five can be right about what they measure. They copied the official data at different dates, divided by different population estimates and used different prices. The error would be to report a number without its source.]{.fact .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The misconception of the act. Policy students in particular will meet conflicting numbers in reports and the press.

The practical rule: pick the source that fits the question (official national accounts for recent U.S. growth; the Penn World Table for cross-country comparisons in PPP; Maddison for the very long run), say which one you used, and check whether the conclusion survives another source.
:::

[Repeat the comparison for **2010 to the last common year**. Are the differences between the sources larger or smaller than for 2000 onwards?]{.tryit}

A good extension: write a small function growth_between(start, end) so that any period is one call away.

## Five habits make a download trustworthy

::: {.incremental}
- **Save what you download**, with the date in the file name.
- **Write down the source, the series code and the date** next to every result.
- **Check the units and the latest date** before you compute anything: `.tail()` is your friend.
- **Keep keys secret**: Colab Secrets, never the notebook.
- **Be polite to the servers**: download once and reuse the table.
:::

::: {.notes}
The good-habits list of B.11. Every Sources note in the book (and every source line on these slides) follows the second habit: producer, series code, and the date of the download.

Citing data: name the producer (BLS, World Bank, IMF), the dataset and its edition (Penn World Table 11.0, Maddison Project Database 2023, WEO October 2026), the series code, and the download date. For research datasets, cite the paper too (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015; Bolt and van Zanden 2024).
:::

## Read the documentation before you trust a series

::: {.incremental}
- **FRED**: the notes under every series chart give the units, the frequency, the seasonal adjustment and the original producer.
- **World Bank**: every indicator page has a definition, a source and its limitations.
- **Penn World Table**: the user guide sits in the file list we downloaded (`pwt110_user_guide_to_data_files.pdf`).
- **Maddison**: the `Notes` and `Sources` sheets of the Excel file.
- **Eurostat, ECB, OECD**: the metadata page of each dataset explains every dimension code.
:::

[Five minutes with the documentation saves an afternoon of wrong results.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
A habit the appendix implies in every section: read the units and the definitions where the producer writes them. The Penn World Table's user guide was in the Dataverse file list of Act V; Maddison's documentation is in the first two sheets of the workbook (which pandas would read by default if you forget sheet_name).

Ask: where would you find out whether FRED's GDPC1 is annualized? (In the notes on its series page: it is a seasonally adjusted annual rate.)
:::

## Cite a dataset as carefully as a paper

::: {.incremental}
- **Who** produced it: the agency or the authors.
- **What**: the dataset and its edition (Penn World Table 11.0; WEO, October 2026).
- **Which series**: the code (`UNRATE`, `NY.GDP.PCAP.KD`).
- **Where**: the link or the DOI. **When**: the download date.
:::

. . .

::: {.eqpanel}
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Unemployment Rate [`UNRATE`], retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, fred.stlouisfed.org/series/UNRATE, 17 October 2026.
:::

::: {.notes}
The example follows the citation format that FRED itself suggests on every series page: producer, title, code, "retrieved from FRED", the address and the date.

For research datasets, cite the paper as well: Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer (2015) for the Penn World Table; Bolt and van Zanden (2024) for the Maddison Project. The source lines on every chart of this deck follow the same pattern.
:::

## When a download fails, fall back on a copy

```python
try:
    unemployment_rate = read_fred("UNRATE")
    print("Downloaded from FRED")
except Exception as problem:
    print("FRED did not answer:", problem)
    unemployment_rate = pd.read_csv(BOOK_DATA + "ch07/fig7-2.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
    print("Using the copy stored in the book's repository instead")
```

. . .

::: {.output}
```text
Downloaded from FRED
```
:::

[Servers are sometimes down, busy or changed. Wait a minute and run the cell again first.]{.comment .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Errors usually arrive as an HTTPError or a ConnectionError. The try/except pattern from the fredapi cell is reused: try the live source; if it fails, print the problem and read the book's prepared copy.

In our run FRED answered, so only the first branch ran. To see the fallback, break the code on purpose (read_fred("UNRATEX")) and run it.
:::

## Predict the fix

[`read_fred("UNRATES")` stops with `HTTPError: HTTP Error 404: Not Found`. What went wrong, and how do you fix it?]{.predict-output}

. . .

[A 404 means the address does not exist: here the series code is misspelled (`UNRATES`). Check the code on the FRED website and copy it exactly.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
A quick debugging exercise before the table of common errors. Ask students to read the error message aloud: the last line of a Python error is the most useful one.

Variants to try: a 403 (add a User-Agent), a ModuleNotFoundError (rerun the install cell).
:::

## Common errors, part 1: installing and addressing {.compact}

| Error message | What it usually means | What to do |
|------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'wbgapi'` | the library is not installed in this session | run the `%pip install` cell again |
| `HTTPError: HTTP Error 404: Not Found` | the web address or the series code is wrong | check the code on the source's website; copy it exactly |
| `HTTPError: HTTP Error 403: Forbidden` | the server refused the program | add a User-Agent, as for Our World in Data |
| `HTTPError: HTTP Error 429` or `503` | too many requests, or the server is busy | wait a minute and try again; download less often |

::: {.notes}
The first half of the appendix's table. The 429 is a rate limit: the server counts your requests and refuses when there are too many. Downloading once and reusing the table (the good habit) avoids it.

A new Colab session forgets every installed library, so ModuleNotFoundError is the first error of almost every session that skips the install cell.
:::

## Common errors, part 2: inside the data {.compact}

| Error message | What it usually means | What to do |
|------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| `KeyError: 'value'` | a column name that does not exist | print `table.columns` and use the exact name |
| an empty table | no data for this combination of codes | check each code of the key; try fewer filters |
| `ValueError` in `pd.read_excel` | wrong sheet name | open the file and check the sheet names |
| an API key error | no key, or a key not visible to the notebook | add it in Colab Secrets and switch on *Notebook access* |

[Read the last line of the error first: it usually names the problem.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The second half of the table. The last row is ours, from the fredapi section: if the secret exists but Notebook access is off, userdata.get fails and the cell skips politely.

Empty tables are the silent error: no message, just nothing. The causes in this deck: SPOO instead of SP00 in an SDMX key, LUR for a country with no unemployment data in the WEO, a Eurostat filter value that does not exist.
:::

## Cheat sheet: one call per source {.compact-xs}

| Source | Library (way) | The call that downloads |
|--------------------|--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| FRED | pandas (4) | `pd.read_csv("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=UNRATE")` |
| FRED | `pandas-datareader` (1) | `web.DataReader(["GDPC1", "PCECC96"], "fred", start="2000-01-01")` |
| FRED | `fredapi` (1, key) | `Fred(api_key=KEY).get_series("GDPC1")` |
| World Bank | `wbgapi` (1) | `wb.data.DataFrame("NY.GDP.PCAP.KD", ["USA", "CHN"], time=range(1960, 2030))` |
| IMF | `imfp` (1) | `imfp.imf_get("WEO", {"COUNTRY": ["USA"], "INDICATOR": "NGDP_RPCH"})` |
| ECB | `sdmx1` (2) | `sdmx.Client("ECB").data("EXR", key={...})` |
| Eurostat | `eurostat` (1) | `eurostat.get_data_df("une_rt_a", filter_pars={...})` |
| OECD, IMF, BIS… | `dbnomics` (3) | `fetch_series("IMF/WEO:latest/USA.NGDP_RPCH.pcent_change")` |
| Penn World Table | pandas (4) | `pd.read_stata("https://dataverse.nl/api/access/datafile/554030")` |
| Maddison | pandas (4) | `pd.read_excel(".../datafile/421302", sheet_name="Full data")` |
| Our World in Data | pandas (4) | `pd.read_csv(chart_address + ".csv", storage_options={"User-Agent": ...})` |

::: {.notes}
A slide to photograph or print. Every call is from this deck (the fredapi line is shortened: in the notebook the key comes from Colab Secrets, never typed).

The search functions are the other half of each library: wb.series.info and wb.economy.info, imfp.imf_get_codelists, sdmx.list_sources, eurostat.get_pars and get_dic, fredapi's search.
:::

## What to remember from this appendix

::: {.incremental}
- **The map**: official collectors (FRED, World Bank, IMF, OECD, Eurostat, ECB, BIS) and research datasets (Penn World Table, Maddison, Our World in Data).
- **Four ways in**: a specialized library, SDMX, a collection, or a file read straight from its address.
- **Every series has a code**: find it first, then check the units and the latest date.
- **Sources differ** because of vintages, population estimates and prices: 1.28% versus 1.11% a year.
- **Record where and when** you got every number; keep keys secret; save a copy.
:::

::: {.notes}
One point per act, more or less: Act I (map and four ways), Acts II–V (codes, units, latest dates), Act VI (sources differ; habits).

Every chapter of the book reads prepared copies of these data from its GitHub repository. With this appendix, students can go back to the original sources, update them, and extend any chapter to other countries and years.
:::
